title: Manitoba wildfire response in 2025 hampered by equipment shortages and fatigue among staff, report concludes
summary: Manitoba was unprepared for the disastrous 2025 wildfire season and needs to devote more money, staff and equipment to ensure it can respond to all manner of emergencies, a new report says.

image.caption: Wildfires at Wanless in spring 2025, a disastrous wildfire season in Manitoba. (AP)

blocks.text: Manitoba
Manitoba was unprepared for the disastrous 2025 wildfire season and needs to devote more money, staff and equipment to ensure it can respond to all manner of emergencies, a new report says.
Province must spend more on people and equipment in order to prepare for future emergencies: document

The 97-page report into the emergency management response for the 2025 wildfires, made public by the province Monday, concluded Manitoba suffered from equipment shortages, staff shortages and poor communication, both among staff members and with the public.

The province also had trouble keeping track of wildfire evacuees, providing accommodations and health services to them, managing fatigue among trained staff and providing psychological support for untrained volunteers, the report said.
Between May and October 2025, 445 wildfires scorched 22,000 square kilometres of the province, which is equivalent to about four per cent of Manitoba's land mass.
Two people died, and almost 33,000 people were displaced from about 12,600 households, with most of the evacuations occurring at First Nations in northern Manitoba.
The report into Manitoba's wildfire response was prepared by Brandon University, with help from the Alberta Emergency Management Agency and the Manitoba Emergency Management Organization.
It concluded trained staff and volunteers in municipalities and First Nations did their best to manage the prolonged burden but ultimately were not prepared for a wildfire season of this magnitude.

items: Northern Manitoba fire chiefs look for new equipment, more volunteers following wildfires

blocks.text: "The duration and scale of the response ... placed sustained pressure on personnel, facilities, accommodation capacity, and co-ordinating organizations," the report stated.

"The experiences gathered through the review reinforce the need for arrangements that can be maintained across extended and concurrent evacuations, including adequate staffing, relief capacity, continuity procedures, suitable facilities and clearly assigned operational responsibilities."
Some of the most acute problems involved "shortages in several categories of critical operational equipment," including wildland pumps, hoses, radios, vehicles and fuel, the report stated.
The lack of resources affected front-line operations, impaired deployment and hampered communications, the report continued.

items: What have Manitoba leaders learned from a summer of wildfire evacuations?

blocks.text: "These challenges were identified by multiple departments and agencies, indicating a systemic preparedness and logistics issue," the report stated.

The report made multiple recommendations, which included spending more money and hiring more staff members to ensure emergency management organizations can better plan for emergencies and respond to them.
Infrastructure Minister Lisa Naylor said the provincial government has accepted all the recommendations.

"It was a really challenging summer, with fires lasting from May until September, and with some communities being evacuated, going home and then being evacuated again," she said in an interview Monday.
"We're looking at expanding our services within Emergency Management Organization and then continuing our work on training."
Naylor would not say whether her government regrets ignoring advice in 2023 from the outgoing Progressive Conservative government to conduct an external review of wildfire preparedness.
The province chose to conduct an internal review instead, based on verbal reports and no written recommendations.

blocks.text: Naylor said she did not recall the province's decision to forego an external review of wildfire preparedness and does not recall any media coverage about this.
"A lot was happening last summer," she said, referring to 2025.
Interim PC Leader Konrad Narth said Monday he is pleased to see the province express a desire to improve wildfire preparedness but wants to know when those improvements will be made.

Eric Reder, a campaigner for the Wilderness Committee, an environmental organization, said he is pleased to see the report attribute the severity of wildfires to climate change but is disappointed the report does not advocate any form of climate action.
"This report doesn't say that we have to act on climate in order to eliminate the fire risk, and that is a critical takeaway from other folks who have looked at the situation," he said.
